A cerebral aneurysm of 7 mm or less has a 5-year risk of rupture of less than 0.1%. The risk of rupture increases with the size of the aneurysm. B

Evaluate for subarachnoid hemorrhage with a noncontrast CT if the patient presents with severe, sudden onset headache with nausea and vomiting, meningismus, altered level of consciousness, and/or focal neurologic deficits. C
Surgical or endovascular treatment of a cerebral aneurysm or aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage should be performed at a high volume center. B

background.definition: Cerebral aneurysm is an abnormal local dilation of a cerebral artery (classified as saccular, fusiform, or dissecting). Subarachnoid hemorrhage is extravasation of blood into the subarachnoid space. Saccular aneurysms (eg, Berry aneurysm) are outpouchings that arise from arterial bifurcation points.

list.listitem: Aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage: 27,000 people per year or 1/10,000/y in the United States.
The female to male ratio is 2:1; it is 2.1 times more common in African Americans. Peak incidence is in the sixth decade.
Cerebral aneurysm: 2% to 5% or 15 million people in the United States. Female to male ratio is 3:2. In a Dutch study, 1.8% of older adults in the general population had an aneurysm.
Incidental cerebral aneurysm is seen in 9% of first-degree relatives; incidental cerebral aneurysm in 4% of first-degree relatives of patients with sporadic subarachnoid hemorrhage.
First-degree relatives of patients who suffered from a subarachnoid hemorrhage are at 3 times the risk of the general population for developing a subarachnoid hemorrhage.
Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease: 5% to 40% of patients have a cerebral aneurysm.
Two percent to 5% of strokes are from an aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage.
Eighty percent of subarachnoid hemorrhages are due to a ruptured cerebral aneurysm.
Multifactorial.
Risk factors for the presence of cerebral aneurysm are shown in the table.

Risk factors associated with cerebral aneurysm hemorrhage include cocaine use, family history (OR = 4.0), cigarette smoking (OR = 3.1), hypertension (OR = 2.6), alcohol consumption, and coarctation of the aorta.
Cerebral aneurysms are structural defects in the tunica media and abnormal hemodynamic shear stresses leading to aneurysm formation and potential rupture of cerebral arteries.
Atherosclerosis typically leads to fusiform aneurysms.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Family history (especially more than one first-degree relative)

list.listitem: Screen for cerebral aneurysm if 2 first-degree relatives have intracranial aneurysms and in patients with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease. B
The preferred study is magnetic resonance angiogram. C
MRA or CTA should be used to evaluate an incidental, asymptomatic cerebral aneurysm. C

Evaluate for subarachnoid hemorrhage with a noncontrast CT if patient presents with severe, sudden onset headache with nausea and vomiting, meningismus, altered level of consciousness, and/or focal neurologic deficits. C
In suspected subarachnoid hemorrhage with negative noncontrast CT, a lumbar puncture should be performed. C
Evaluate for cerebral vasospasm after subarachnoid hemorrhage with transcranial ultrasound. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Band-like pressure around the head, associated with muscle stiffness
May have an aura; personal or family history of migraines
Usually unilateral in temporal region, associated with ipsilateral lacrimation, nasal congestion, and conjunctival injection
Recent upper respiratory infection, fever, petechial rash
Patient usually older than 60 years, usually unilateral in the temporal region, associated with jaw claudication
Acute onset, unilateral facial drooping, paresis, loss of sensation, headache less common
Usually with preceding constitutional symptoms of fever, malaise, myalgia

list.listitem: Cerebral aneurysm: usually asymptomatic but may cause headache, decreased vision, cranial nerve III palsy, facial pain. Subarachnoid hemorrhage is the presenting symptom of cerebral aneurysm 58% of the time.

Aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage: sudden onset headache (classically described as "worst headache of my life"), syncope, altered mental status, seizure, nausea/vomiting, meningismus, retinal subhyaloid hemorrhage.

Sentinel headache is a sudden and severe headache that precedes a subarachnoid hemorrhage by 6 to 20 days; it occurs in 10% to 43% of aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhages. Thunderclap headache is a rapid onset of a very severe almost debilitating headache with no apparent cause; may be a warning sign of a pending medical emergency, ie, intracranial hemorrhage.
Terson's syndrome is an intravitreous hemorrhage associated with subarachnoid hemorrhage; associated with a poor prognosis.

Xanthochromia is yellowish discoloration of cerebrospinal fluid representing bilirubin from the breakdown of hemoglobin indicative of a subarachnoid hemorrhage; usually occurs 12 hours after a subarachnoid hemorrhage.
While the reference standard test is digital subtraction angiography, less invasive options for detecting cerebral aneurysms include CT angiography, MRA, and transcranial Doppler ultrasound.
AHA/ASA guidelines (2023) recommend that for symptomatic patients with suspected hemorrhage, the recommended initial study is CT of the head without contrast ().

CT and MRA are similar in accuracy, and either is an option for detection of aneurysms in asymptomatic patients, as in a patient with polycystic kidney disease or first-degree relative(s) with aneurysm ().
Transcranial Doppler is less sensitive and specific and is typically used to detect vasospasm after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage.
Lumbar puncture suggests subarachnoid hemorrhage if there is xanthochromia or elevated RBCs that fail to clear; RBCs clear in traumatic tap.
See algorithm in .

The Ottawa subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) risk score has been externally validated and identifies patients at very low risk of SAH. Its use for initial risk stratification is recommended by AHA/ASA guidelines (2023).
Surgical or endovascular treatment should be performed at a high volume center that has a neurosurgical, interventional neuroradiologic, and neurologic department. B

Endovascular coiling has better outcomes than surgical clipping for treatment of cerebral aneurysms and aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhages (lower inpatient mortality, shorter hospital stay, and lower treatment cost). B
Nimodopine prophylaxis improves outcomes after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (NNT to prevent one poor outcome = 20). B
Antiplatelet therapy is often recommended following coil embolization of aneursyms, but may be discontinued after 2 years and favorable MR angiography evaluation.

AHA/ASA guidelines (2023) recommend that patients with seizures following treatment of aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (aSAH) should receive anti-seizure medications for 7 days. Phenytoin should be avoided, though. Prophylactic use of seizure medication can be considered in patients with ruptured middle cerebral artery aneursym, high grade aSAH, hydrocephalus, or cortical infarct.

Nimodipine deli vered enterally helps prevent delayed cerebral ischemia and improves outcomes in patients following aSAH, and is recommended. Routine use of statins or IV magnesium is not recommended.

Surgical or endovascular treatment of a cerebral aneurysm or aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage should be performed at a high volume center that has a neurosurgical, interventional neuroradiologic, and neurologic department, as well as a dedicated Neurologic Critical Care Unit. B

An option for cerebral aneurysms that are smaller than 7 mm with no history of subarachnoid hemorrhage is observation. Physician evaluation and imaging should be scheduled at regular intervals (CTA or MRA yearly for 2-3 years initially, and then every 2-5 years thereafter).
For surgical repair of cerebral aneurysm, options include craniotomy with clip ligation (clipping) or endovascular coiling.

Clipping is done by a neurosurgeon under general anesthesia. Clips are placed across the neck of the aneurysm and exclude it from circulation permanently. Morbidity and mortality are as high as 15.7% and 3%, respectively.

Endovascular coiling is done by a neuroradiologist, a neurosurgeon, or an interventionally trained neurologist under general anesthesia or sedation. Detachable platinum coils of different shapes and sizes are deployed through a microcatheter to fill up the aneurysm and stop blood flow. Morbidity and mortality 3.7% to 5.3% and 1.1% to 1.5%, respectively. It is not feasible to perform coiling in up to 1 in 7 aneurysms.

Endovascular coiling has been shown to have fewer harms than surgical clipping for treatment of cerebral aneurysms and aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhages (lower inpatient mortality, shorter hospital stay) and lower treatment cost. Coiling has been recommended over clipping in patients presenting in good clinical condition; no evidence-based recommendation exists for patients presenting in poor condition. However, there is a higher rate of rebleeding among aneurysms treated with coiling versus clipping and lower occlusion rates. A meta-analysis of 11 studies of clipping found a success rate for occlusion of 89% (95% CI 85% to 92%) compared with 54% (95% CI 50% to 57%) for 17 studies of coiling. Rates of favorable neurologic outcome were similar (95% to 97%)

Flow-diverters like the Pipeline device are placed in the parent artery at the aneurysm neck. They disrupt intra-aneurysmal flow to induce intra-aneurysmal thrombosis. A retrospective cohort study with 581 patients with mostly anterior circulation (90%) and saccular aneurysms (86%) found that found that the complete occlusion rate was 89% at 2 years, with 94% good neurological outcome.
For treatment of aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage, the rates of neurologic incapacity or death are 30.6% with clipping and 23.7% with coiling.
There is insufficient evidence to support routine use of intraoperative cooling for patients with subarachnoid hemorrhage from aneurysm treated with surgery.
Consider stool softeners to help avoid excessive straining.

Cerebral vasospasm: this occurs in 20% to 30% of patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage and is the leading cause of death. It typically occurs 3 to 12 days after bleed; clinical signs of vasospasm include a decline in neurologic function or a new focal neurologic deficit; evaluate by transcranial Doppler ultrasonography. Nimodipine prophylaxis at 60 mg q4h for 21 days has been shown to improve the odds of a good outcome compared with placebo by 1.86 (99% CI, 1.07-3.25) and to decrease the risk of developing a neurologic deficit and mortality associated with vasospasm (odds ratio = 0.46). Nimodipine reduced cerebral infarction rate on CT (odds ratio = 0.58; 99% CI, 0.38-0.90).

Neurologic deterioration: triple-H therapy (hypertension, hypervolemia, and hemodilution) may be used after surgical treatment of the aneurysm; goals include hypertension to reverse neurologic deficits (via pressors), a central venous pressure of 8 to 12 mm Hg (via intravenous fluid), and a hematocrit of 30%. Note: persistent vasospasm, despite Triple-H therapy, has been treated successfully with angioplasty, intraarterial papaverine, or intrathecal nitroprusside.
Hydrocephalus: occurs in 15% to 20% of patients; managed with ventriculostomy.

Cardiac abnormalities: elevation in CK-MB and troponin I in up to 20% of patients; mechanism of myocardial injury probably due to centrally mediated release of catecholamines. Common ECG findings include ST depression, QT prolongation, and T wave inversion.
Rebleeding, seizures, and hyponatremia may also occur.
A cerebral aneurysm of 7 mm or smaller has a 5-year risk of rupture of less than 0.1%. The risk of rupture increases with aneurysm size. B
A poor outcome after clipping or coiling an unruptured cerebral aneurysm is associated with increasing patient age, aneurysm size, and location in the posterior circulation. B

The 5-year rate of rupture in anterior circulation and posterior circulation cerebral aneurysms are (respectively): less than 7 mm = less than 0.1% for both; 7- to 12-mm aneurysms = 2.6% and 14.5%; 13- to 24-mm aneurysms = 14.5% and 18.4%; and 25-mm or larger aneurysms = 40% and 50%. Other studies suggest that aneurysms less than 3 to 6 mm have a low rupture rate (≤0.5%/year) while those >10 mm have a high rate (4.4 to 33%/year).
Eighty-five percent of cerebral aneurysms occur in the anterior circulation.

Combined surgery-related morbidity and mortality of unruptured cerebral aneurysm at 1 year depends on patient age: younger than 45 years = 6.5%, 45 to 64 years old = 14.4%, and older than 64 years = 32%.

Aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage: 15% will die prior to reaching the hospital; 35% will die within 30 days of the event; 25% will have a permanent neurologic deficit; and 25% will have a "good result."
The Hunt and Hess scale predicts surgical risk for aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage ().

The Fisher scale predicts likelihood of cerebral vasospasm (and worse prognosis) following an aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage based upon hemorrhage pattern on initial CT (most commonly will develop vasospasm with grade 3 or 4); Grade 1: no blood detected; Grade 2: vertical layer of blood less than 1 mm thick; Grade 3: vertical layer of blood 1 mm or more in thickness; Grade 4: intracerebral or intraventricular clots with or without subarachnoid blood.

Risk of a second distinct aneurysm after an initial episode include age less than 60 years, female sex at birth, tobacco use, a positive family history, more than one aneurysm at initial diagnosis, and aneurysm in the middle cerebral artery.
If a small cerebral aneurysm is clinically and radiographically stable, monitor via CTA or MRA yearly for 2 to 3 years, and then every 2 to 5 years thereafter.
Patients with cerebral aneurysm should avoid smoking, consuming large amounts of alcohol, stimulant medications, illicit drugs, and excessive straining or valsalva maneuvers.

feature.caption: The Hunt and Hess Scale to Predict Surgical Risk for Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage.
feature.feature_body:
Grade Signs/Symptoms Survival Rate (%)
1 Asymptomatic or mild headache with slight nuchal rigidity 70
2 Severe headache with nuchal rigidity, no neurologic deficit except a cranial nerve palsy 60
3 Drowsy or confused, minimal neurologic deficit 50
4 Stuporous, hemiparesis 20
5 Coma, decerebrate posturing 10
